newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Allianz sticks to bullish outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Allianz sticks to bullish outlook.

text.p: Europe's leading insurance group, Allianz AG Holding, on Monday said it was still on track for record earnings this year after its premium income rose 8.3 percent in the first six months of 1996.

Henning Schulte-Noelle, chairman of the Munich-based insurer, told Allianz's annual shareholder meeting that overall foreign business had been buoyant so far despite price pressures plaguing the German market.

"Your company is progressing well. We are making particular progress towards strengthening our earnings power," Schulte-Noelle said, promising shareholders that the group's current dividend level of 16 marks would be at least maintained.
Schulte-Noelle said he expected a considerable boost in pre-tax earnings in 1996 but added his customary caveat that progress depended on claims and capital market developments.
Allianz's pre-tax earnings surged 34.4 percent to a record 3.04 billion marks ($2 billion) in 1995 and Schulte-Noelle has in the past forecast another double-digit rise in earnings this year.

However, the group does not see net earnings keeping pace with the pre-tax figure. Allianz's net profit was 2.02 billion marks in 1995, boosted sharply by one-off tax breaks related to its east German business.
The news depressed Allianz's shares marginally, sending them down five marks to 2,755 marks in bourse trade.

"This is all positive news but there were no big surprises here," said BHF Bank analyst Dieter Hein. "Allianz has done extremely well in the run-up to these numbers and it might even be natural to see a small decline."
Schulte-Noelle said he expected Allianz's premium income to rise about six percent by the end of the year, compared with the seven percent rise to 70.5 billion marks achieved in 1995.

The insurer's premium income advanced 8.3 percent to 39.6 billion marks in the first six months of 1996, notwithstanding a muted German market where premiums rose by only one percent to 21.4 billion marks.
Allianz's business has been plagued in the past year by stiff price competition for auto insurance cover on its newly deregulated home market.

But foreign business compensated, especially on the life insurance side. Allianz said its non-German European life and health insurance premiums rose as much as 28 percent in the first six months of the year.

The forecasts do not allow for any effects of possible consolidation of new units. Allianz is expected to shortly complete its takeover of the Vereinte Gruppe, Europe's number two in health insurance, whose fate has hung in the balance since Allianz acquired it in a package from Swiss Re in 1994.
Schulte-Noelle said he expected full European Union cartel approval for its Vereinte takeover by the end of 1996.

Allianz was expected to sell Vereinte because of cartel concerns about its role in European health insurance, but opted in July to keep the group and sell its DKV health insurance unit to Muenchener Rueckversicherungs AG.
Allianz gained Munich Re's 25 percent stake in Vereinte Krankenversicherung, a majority stake in the Hermes loan insurance group and other small stakes as part of the deal.

As part of its drive toward increased transparency, Allianz also revealed for the first time its shareholdings below five percent in major German and international companies -- which it said had a total market value of 3.744 billion marks.
The firms listed, none of which surprised analysts, included Germany's Siemens and Daimler-Benz as well as Banco Popular of Spain and Italy's Credito Italiano.
